Flooding Disrupts Oil & Gas Operations in Ecuador's Oriente Basin

Heavy rainfall has triggered widespread flooding across Ecuador’s northeastern Oriente Basin, severely impacting oil and gas production and transport in the region. Key industry sources report that rising river levels since Tuesday have inundated access roads and production facilities, restricting the movement of personnel and equipment. The situation remains fluid, with additional rainfall forecast and floodwaters yet to recede.

Among the operators affected is Consorcio Shushufindi SA, which confirmed on Thursday that several of its field installations have been partially evacuated as a precaution. “Floods have cut off access to at least three of our key well pads, and we are currently operating with reduced staff to ensure safety,” said a spokesperson for the company. “While production continues at a limited rate, we are closely monitoring the situation and are prepared to implement further shutdowns if conditions worsen.”

According to data from the Ecuadorian Hydrocarbon Association, the affected area accounts for roughly 30% of the country’s onshore crude output. Preliminary estimates suggest that daily production across the region is down by 18% since the onset of flooding, a figure that could rise if rainfall persists. “Logistical challenges are mounting,” said Hugo Vélez, a Quito-based oil sector analyst. “Flooded roads have delayed the delivery of essential supplies and are hampering maintenance crews’ ability to reach critical infrastructure.”

Local authorities in Sucumbíos and Orellana provinces have declared states of alert, as emergency workers focus on reinforcing levees near major oil transport arteries. The main export pipeline, which traverses several flood-affected zones, remains operational but at reduced throughput. “Our teams are patrolling the pipeline route and making contingency plans should water levels threaten the integrity of the line,” said an operations manager from PetroAndes, another operator in the basin.

Workers’ unions have raised concerns about the safety of field personnel. “Some workers have had to remain on-site longer than scheduled because roads are impassable,” said Luis Medina, regional coordinator for the Petroleum Workers’ Union. “We urge all companies to prioritize evacuations and support for their staff.”

With weather forecasts predicting continued heavy rain into the weekend, industry observers warn that recovery efforts may be protracted. “It’s a complex situation that underscores the vulnerability of the sector’s infrastructure to extreme weather events,” Vélez noted. “Contingency plans and rapid response will be critical in minimizing further disruption.”

As of Thursday afternoon, the full extent of the damage remains unclear, with operators and authorities continuing to assess the evolving situation.
